analysis.one_liner: Caps yearly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 per person, $4,000 per family.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat with three House committees since its April 1, 2025 introduction, with no committee vote and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a hard ceiling on how much people pay out of pocket for prescription drugs each year: no more than $2,000 per person or $4,000 per family, starting in 2026, with the limit rising after that with medical inflation. It applies the cap to Affordable Care Act marketplace plans and, through parallel changes to existing law, to employer-based health plans too. Today, many job-based plans let drug costs count against out-of-pocket maximums that run far higher, so the cap mainly protects people with expensive medications for conditions like cancer, diabetes, and autoimmune disease.
analysis.who_benefits: People who take expensive prescription drugs, especially those with chronic or serious illnesses who today can hit out-of-pocket maximums several times the proposed cap. Family coverage gets extra protection at $4,000.

how_it_helps.text: Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $2,000 per individual and $4,000 per family for plan years beginning in 2026, and indexes the limit to rise with the medical component of the consumer price index in later years.
Applies the cap to ACA-qualified health plans and, through new provisions in the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code, to employer group health plans as well.
Takes effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored plans absorb the difference when drug cost-sharing would otherwise exceed the cap. Some of that cost could show up in premiums or employer contributions; the bill does not lower drug prices themselves, it limits what patients pay for them.

drawbacks.text: The cap shifts costs rather than lowering them: drug makers keep their prices, and insurers and employers bear the difference, which could be passed back into premiums or wages.
Employers offering group coverage face a new federal mandate on plan design starting in 2026, which small and self-insured employers would have to absorb or adjust benefits around.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people facing four- or five-figure annual drug bills, a firm $2,000/$4,000 cap is a large, direct benefit. The cost is real but diffuse: insurers and employers pay the difference, and since the bill does nothing about underlying drug prices, the pressure shows up in premiums over time. An honest supporter would acknowledge that a price cap without price negotiation leaves the root cause untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford introduced the Capping Prescription Costs Act of 2025 in the House on April 1, 2025.

The bill was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means; under House rules the Speaker assigned it for consideration of provisions falling within each committee's jurisdiction.
Nine members, all House Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
No committee has reported the bill, and there has been no floor vote or further action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome preserves the status quo: health insurers and employer health plans continue to set drug cost-sharing under current rules, and no one bears the cap's cost. Patients with expensive prescriptions get no relief until a version of this idea actually becomes law.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors are House Democrats, and with Republicans holding House and committee majorities in the 119th Congress, the bill has no path without Republican support.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to cap what patients pay for covered drugs at $2,000/$4,000, absorbing costs they can currently shift to enrollees. Their interest in keeping cost-sharing flexible runs against the patients the cap protects.
Group health plans face a new mandate to cap employee drug cost-sharing beginning in 2026, a plan-design cost borne largely by employers and secondarily by workers in premiums.

The bill does not lower drug prices, so manufacturers keep their current revenues; more affordable plans may even expand access to their products. But greater insurer pressure on prices could follow as plans absorb more of the tab.

analysis.trajectory: With three committee referrals and no action from any of them, the bill's most likely path in the current Congress is to remain in committee until the session ends, as happens with the large majority of House bills that lack support from the chamber's majority party.
